claim: Osteoporosis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide.
source: Osteoporosis, a disease characterized by porous bone prone to fractures, affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide (Cooper and Ferrari, 2019; Hernlund et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cooper and Ferrari, 2019 and Hernlund et al., 2013

claim: The global annual incidence of bone fragility fractures was 9 million in the year 2000.
source: Most recent estimates place the global annual incidence of bone fragility fractures at 9 million in the year 2000 (Cooper and Ferrari, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper and Ferrari, 2019

claim: Projections for the year 2050 suggest between 7 and 21 million annual hip fractures.
source: projections for the year 2050 suggest between 7 and 21 million annual hip fractures (Gullberg et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gullberg et al., 1997

claim: Osteoporosis-associated bone fractures lead to disabilities, pain, and increased mortality.
source: Osteoporosis-associated bone fractures lead to disabilities, pain, and increased mortality (Cooper and Ferrari, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cooper and Ferrari, 2019

claim: In the United States, medical cost for osteoporosis was estimated at US$17 billion in 2005.
source: In the United States, medical cost for osteoporosis, including inpatient, outpatient, and long-term care costs, has been estimated at US$17 billion in 2005 (Burge et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Burge et al., 2007

claim: In the European Union, the total cost of osteoporosis is projected to rise from about €100 billion in 2010 to €120 billion in 2025.
source: in the European Union, the total cost of osteoporosis, including pharmacological interventions and loss of quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), is projected to rise from about €100 billion in 2010 to €120 billion in 2025 (Odén et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Odén et al., 2013

claim: Osteoporotic bone is the consequence of an imbalance of continuous bone resorption and bone formation.
source: Osteoporotic bone is the consequence of an imbalance of continuous bone resorption and bone formation, which—under close to homeostatic conditions—has the function to remove microfractures and renew the structural integrity of bone.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of osteoporosis pathophysiology

claim: Postmenopausal women are particularly at risk of osteoporosis.
source: Postmenopausal women are particularly at risk of osteoporosis: the rapid decline of systemic estrogen levels after menopause and other aging-related effects such as increased oxidative stress contribute to or drive the development of osteoporosis (Riggs et al., 1998; Manolagas, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Riggs et al., 1998 and Manolagas, 2010

claim: The rapid decline of systemic estrogen levels after menopause contributes to or drives the development of osteoporosis.
source: the rapid decline of systemic estrogen levels after menopause and other aging-related effects such as increased oxidative stress contribute to or drive the development of osteoporosis (Riggs et al., 1998; Manolagas, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Riggs et al., 1998 and Manolagas, 2010

claim: Aging-related effects such as increased oxidative stress contribute to or drive the development of osteoporosis.
source: the rapid decline of systemic estrogen levels after menopause and other aging-related effects such as increased oxidative stress contribute to or drive the development of osteoporosis (Riggs et al., 1998; Manolagas, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Riggs et al., 1998 and Manolagas, 2010

claim: Osteoporosis can be a sequela of diseases affecting bone metabolism and remodeling such as primary hyperparathyroidism or gastrointestinal diseases.
source: Moreover, osteoporosis can be a sequela of diseases affecting bone metabolism and remodeling such as primary hyperparathyroidism or gastrointestinal diseases (Painter et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Painter et al., 2006

claim: Glucocorticoid administration is the most common cause of secondary osteoporosis.
source: as a prime example, glucocorticoid administration is the most common cause of secondary osteoporosis (Weinstein, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinstein, 2012

claim: Over the last decades, an array of different osteoporosis treatments have emerged, from simple dietary supplementations such as calcium and vitamin D to specialized drugs targeting bone-forming and -resorbing cells and related signaling pathways.
source: Over the last decades, an array of different osteoporosis treatments have emerged, from simple dietary supplementations such as calcium and vitamin D to specialized drugs targeting bone-forming and -resorbing cells and related signaling pathways (Tu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tu et al., 2018

claim: Very few treatment schemes have been clinically tested so far when compared to the total number of available options.
source: Due to the huge number of such treatment schemes and the required time from study inception to completion, very few of them have been clinically tested so far when compared to the total number of available options.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the large number of possible treatment combinations and practical limitations of clinical trials

claim: Lemaire et al., 2004 describes the dynamics of bone-forming and -resorbing cell populations coupled through signaling pathways.
source: Pioneering work by Lemaire et al., 2004 describes the dynamics of bone-forming and -resorbing cell populations coupled through signaling pathways and could qualitatively reproduce the effects of senescence, glucocorticoid excess, and estrogen and vitamin D deficiency on bone turnover.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaire et al., 2004

claim: The model by Lemaire et al., 2004 could qualitatively reproduce the effects of senescence, glucocorticoid excess, and estrogen and vitamin D deficiency on bone turnover.
source: Pioneering work by Lemaire et al., 2004 describes the dynamics of bone-forming and -resorbing cell populations coupled through signaling pathways and could qualitatively reproduce the effects of senescence, glucocorticoid excess, and estrogen and vitamin D deficiency on bone turnover.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaire et al., 2004

claim: Compartment-based descriptions of the mineral metabolism, bone-forming and -resorbing cell populations, and related signaling factors have elucidated the role of essential regulatory mechanisms underlying mineral balance and bone turnover.
source: Since then, compartment-based descriptions of the mineral metabolism, bone-forming and -resorbing cell populations, and related signaling factors have elucidated the role of essential regulatory mechanisms underlying mineral balance and bone turnover (Komarova et al., 2003; Lemaire et al., 2004; Pivonka et al., 2008; Pivonka et al., 2010; Peterson and Riggs, 2010; Zumsande et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011; Graham et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2014; Komarova et al., 2015; Berkhout et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to modeling studies

claim: An integrated mathematical framework for multiple drugs, which can also be used to quantitatively predict the effects of drug combinations in sequence and in parallel is not yet available.
source: An integrated mathematical framework for multiple drugs, which can also be used to quantitatively predict the effects of drug combinations in sequence and in parallel is not yet available.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature and identification of a gap in current modeling approaches

claim: The authors calibrate and validate the model using data from several clinical trials.
source: Using data from several clinical trials, we calibrate and validate the model, demonstrating its predictive capacity for complex medication scenarios, including sequential and parallel drug combinations.
evidence: This describes the methodology and validation approach used in the study

claim: The model demonstrates predictive capacity for complex medication scenarios, including sequential and parallel drug combinations.
source: Using data from several clinical trials, we calibrate and validate the model, demonstrating its predictive capacity for complex medication scenarios, including sequential and parallel drug combinations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript supported by the validation results

claim: There is a large potential to improve gains in bone mineral density by exploiting synergistic interactions between different drug classes, without increasing the total amount of drug administered.
source: Via simulations, we reveal that there is a large potential to improve gains in bone mineral density by exploiting synergistic interactions between different drug classes, without increasing the total amount of drug administered.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation results presented in the manuscript

claim: Bone is constantly turned over to renew its integrity and remove microdamage, at an average rate of about 4% per year in cortical bone and about 30% per year in trabecular bone.
source: As a composite tissue comprising hydroxyapatite, collagen, other proteins, and water (Boskey, 2013), bone is constantly turned over to renew its integrity and remove microdamage, at an average rate of about 4% per year in cortical bone and about 30% per year in trabecular bone (Manolagas, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boskey, 2013 and Manolagas, 2000

claim: Bone is a composite tissue comprising hydroxyapatite, collagen, other proteins, and water.
source: As a composite tissue comprising hydroxyapatite, collagen, other proteins, and water (Boskey, 2013), bone is constantly turned over to renew its integrity and remove microdamage
evidence: Supported by citation to Boskey, 2013

claim: Bone resorption is performed by osteoclasts, multinucleated cells formed through the differentiation and fusion of their immediate precursors (pre-osteoclasts).
source: Bone resorption is performed by osteoclasts, multinucleated cells formed through the differentiation and fusion of their immediate precursors (pre-osteoclasts), which are derived from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells via the myeloid lineage (Boyce and Xing, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyce and Xing, 2008

claim: Pre-osteoclasts are derived from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells via the myeloid lineage.
source: Bone resorption is performed by osteoclasts, multinucleated cells formed through the differentiation and fusion of their immediate precursors (pre-osteoclasts), which are derived from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells via the myeloid lineage (Boyce and Xing, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyce and Xing, 2008

claim: Osteoclasts attach to bone tissue and resorb it through the secretion of hydrogen ions and bone-degrading enzymes.
source: Osteoclasts attach to bone tissue and resorb it through the secretion of hydrogen ions and bone-degrading enzymes (Fuller and Chambers, 1995), which leads to the release of minerals and signaling factors stored in the bone matrix.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuller and Chambers, 1995

claim: Osteoclast activity leads to the release of minerals and signaling factors stored in the bone matrix.
source: Osteoclasts attach to bone tissue and resorb it through the secretion of hydrogen ions and bone-degrading enzymes (Fuller and Chambers, 1995), which leads to the release of minerals and signaling factors stored in the bone matrix.
evidence: Based on inference from the mechanism of bone resorption and citation to Fuller and Chambers, 1995

claim: New bone is formed by osteoblasts, a cell type derived from mesenchymal stem cells via several intermediate states that give rise to pre-osteoblasts and finally osteoblasts.
source: New bone is formed by osteoblasts, a cell type derived from mesenchymal stem cells via several intermediate states that give rise to pre-osteoblasts and finally osteoblasts (Eriksen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eriksen, 2010

claim: Groups of osteoblasts organize into cell clusters (osteons) and collectively lay down an organic matrix (osteoid), which subsequently becomes mineralized over the course of months.
source: Groups of osteoblasts organize into cell clusters (osteons) and collectively lay down an organic matrix (osteoid), which subsequently becomes mineralized over the course of months.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of bone formation physiology

claim: Osteoblasts that are enclosed in the newly secreted bone matrix become osteocytes, nondividing cells with an average life span of up to several decades.
source: Osteoblasts that are enclosed in the newly secreted bone matrix become osteocytes, nondividing cells with an average life span of up to several decades.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of osteocyte biology

claim: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts organize into spatially defined local clusters termed 'bone remodeling units' (BRUs).
source: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts organize into spatially defined local clusters termed 'bone remodeling units' (BRUs) (Figure 1), in which osteoblasts replenish the bone matrix previously resorbed by osteoclasts with a delay of several weeks.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: In bone remodeling units, osteoblasts replenish the bone matrix previously resorbed by osteoclasts with a delay of several weeks.
source: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts organize into spatially defined local clusters termed 'bone remodeling units' (BRUs) (Figure 1), in which osteoblasts replenish the bone matrix previously resorbed by osteoclasts with a delay of several weeks.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of bone remodeling dynamics

claim: In cortical bone, BRUs migrate as a whole in 'tunnels'.
source: In cortical bone, the outer protective bone layer, BRUs migrate as a whole in 'tunnels,' whereas within the inner cancellous bone, BRUs propagate on the surfaces of the trabeculae, renewing the bone matrix in the process (Eriksen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eriksen, 2010

claim: Within the inner cancellous bone, BRUs propagate on the surfaces of the trabeculae, renewing the bone matrix in the process.
source: In cortical bone, the outer protective bone layer, BRUs migrate as a whole in 'tunnels,' whereas within the inner cancellous bone, BRUs propagate on the surfaces of the trabeculae, renewing the bone matrix in the process (Eriksen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eriksen, 2010

claim: Osteoclast formation and activity are prominently regulated by RANKL and macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) synthesized by bone marrow stromal cells.
source: Osteoclast formation and activity are prominently regulated by RANKL and macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF) synthesized by bone marrow stromal cells.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge of osteoclast regulation

claim: When laying down new bone, osteoblasts store signaling factors in the bone matrix, including transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), insulin growth factors (IGFs), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and fibroblast growth factors (FGFs).
source: When laying down new bone, osteoblasts store signaling factors in the bone matrix, including transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), insulin growth factors (IGFs), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), and fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) (Solheim, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solheim, 1998

claim: Upon bone resorption, signaling factors stored in the bone matrix are released and regulate cell fates and activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, thereby coupling bone resorption and formation.
source: Upon bone resorption, these factors are released and regulate cell fates and activity of osteoblasts and osteoclasts, thereby coupling bone resorption and formation (Houde et al., 2009; Eriksen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Houde et al., 2009 and Eriksen, 2010

claim: Osteocytes secrete sclerostin, a Wnt inhibitor interfering with extracellular binding of Wnt ligands.
source: Osteocytes secrete sclerostin, a Wnt inhibitor interfering with extracellular binding of Wnt ligands (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: Sclerostin inhibits bone formation and promotes resorption via downregulation of osteoblastogenesis and upregulation of osteoclastogenesis.
source: Sclerostin inhibits bone formation and promotes resorption via downregulation of osteoblastogenesis and upregulation of osteoclastogenesis (Delgado-Calle et al., 2017; Maré et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delgado-Calle et al., 2017 and Maré et al., 2020

claim: Regulators of calcium homeostasis such as PTH and vitamin D strongly affect the balance of bone formation and resorption alongside the intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium.
source: Since bone also acts as a mineral reservoir for the body, regulators of calcium homeostasis such as PTH and vitamin D also strongly affect the balance of bone formation and resorption alongside the intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium (Mundy and Guise, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mundy and Guise, 1999

claim: Estrogen inhibits bone resorption by inducing apoptosis of osteoclasts.
source: The sex hormone estrogen inhibits bone resorption by inducing apoptosis of osteoclasts (Kameda et al., 1997) and lowering circulating sclerostin levels (Mödder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kameda et al., 1997

claim: Estrogen lowers circulating sclerostin levels.
source: The sex hormone estrogen inhibits bone resorption by inducing apoptosis of osteoclasts (Kameda et al., 1997) and lowering circulating sclerostin levels (Mödder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mödder et al., 2011

claim: The model comprises dynamic components including cell densities of pre-osteoclasts, osteoclasts, pre-osteoblasts, osteoblasts, osteocytes, sclerostin concentration, total bone density, and bone mineral content (BMC).
source: Our model comprises the following dynamic components to describe the bone turnover through a representative BRU: cell densities of (i) pre-osteoclasts, (ii) osteoclasts, (iii) pre-osteoblasts, (iv) osteoblasts, (v) osteocytes, (vi) sclerostin concentration, (vii) total bone density, and (viii) bone mineral content (BMC).
evidence: This describes the structure of the model developed in the study

claim: The BMD is given by the product of bone density and BMC.
source: The BMD is given by the product of bone density and BMC.
evidence: This describes a mathematical relationship in the model

claim: The effects of aging and the onset of menopause are represented through an age-dependent serum estrogen concentration, which has been determined from the literature.
source: The effects of aging and the onset of menopause are represented through an age-dependent serum estrogen concentration, which has been determined from the literature (Sowers et al., 2008; Appendix 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sowers et al., 2008 and reference to Appendix 1

claim: PTH is known to exert anabolic or catabolic effects depending on whether administration is intermittent or continuous.
source: PTH is known to exert anabolic or catabolic effects depending on whether administration is intermittent or continuous (Tam et al., 1982; Hock and Gera, 1992)
evidence: Supported by citations to Tam et al., 1982 and Hock and Gera, 1992

claim: PTH description in the model is restricted to the anabolic administration regimes relevant for osteoporosis treatment.
source: PTH description in our model is restricted to the anabolic administration regimes relevant for osteoporosis treatment.
evidence: This describes a design choice in the model development

claim: The model was calibrated using published clinical data from various seminal studies on both long-term BMD age dependence and the response of BMD and BTMs to the administration of different drugs.
source: We calibrated the model using published clinical data from various seminal studies on both (i) long-term BMD age dependence and (ii) the response of BMD and BTMs to the administration of different drugs (see Appendix 3—table 2 for a comprehensive list of data sources).
evidence: This describes the calibration methodology used in the study

claim: Model calibration yielded an inferred value of about 6% per year on average for skeletal bone turnover, of the same order of values reported for cortical bone, which constitutes about 75% of the skeleton.
source: Without constraining the average rate of skeletal bone turnover, model calibration yielded an inferred value of about 6% per year on average, of the same order of values reported for cortical bone, which constitutes about 75% of the skeleton (Manolagas, 2000).
evidence: This is a finding from the model calibration, compared to literature values from Manolagas, 2000

claim: The model was able to capture the BMD and BTM dynamics across all calibration datasets with remarkable accuracy.
source: The model was able to capture the BMD and BTM dynamics across all calibration datasets with remarkable accuracy (Appendix 3—figure 1), despite the model's structural simplicity.
evidence: This is a finding from the calibration results, supported by data shown in Appendix 3—figure 1

claim: The MAPE for BMD was consistently below 1% for all calibration datasets.
source: To quantify the goodness of the fit, we computed the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) between model simulations and clinical data; the MAPE for BMD was consistently below 1% for all calibration datasets (Appendix 3—table 3), indicating an excellent agreement between model and data.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the calibration analysis, with data in Appendix 3—table 3

claim: The qualitative behavior of BTMs (i.e., the direction of their excursions from baseline) was captured correctly in all calibration datasets.
source: The qualitative behavior of BTMs (i.e., the direction of their excursions from baseline) was captured correctly in all calibration datasets, indicating an adequate description of the drugs' mode of action in the model
evidence: This is a finding from the calibration results

claim: With the single set of previously determined parameters, the model showed a remarkable capacity to quantitatively forecast the effects of a multitude of medication schemes, both during treatment and follow-up periods.
source: With the single set of previously determined parameters, the model showed a remarkable capacity to quantitatively forecast the effects of a multitude of medication schemes, both during treatment and follow-up periods (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Across all validation datasets, MAPEs for BMD were consistently below 1.5%.
source: Across all validation datasets, MAPEs for BMD were consistently below 1.5% (Appendix 3—table 3), indicating an excellent predictive capacity of the model.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the validation analysis, with data in Appendix 3—table 3

claim: The outcomes of different medication sequences were markedly different despite the same total amount of drug administered.
source: Indeed, we found that the outcomes of different medication sequences were markedly different despite the same total amount of drug administered (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Some sequences (such as ARD and RAD) reached a considerably higher maximum BMD during the course of the simulated treatment.
source: Some sequences (such as ARD and RAD) reached a considerably higher maximum BMD during the course of the simulated treatment, which allowed us to rank treatments according to maximum BMD gain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3B

claim: While some sequences were superior to others as measured by the maximum BMD increase during treatment, they performed markedly worse with regard to long-term BMD evolution as predicted by model simulations.
source: Notably, while some sequences were superior to others as measured by the maximum BMD increase during treatment, they performed markedly worse (as compared to, e.g., DRA and RDA) with regard to long-term BMD evolution as predicted by model simulations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Short-term BMD gains may be limited as a proxy for the clinical benefit of a treatment as a whole.
source: This behavior suggests that short-term BMD gains may be limited as a proxy for the clinical benefit of a treatment as a whole.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing differential short-term vs. long-term outcomes

claim: Simulated drug-mediated inhibition of osteoclastogenesis leads to a build-up of an undifferentiated osteoclast precursor pool.
source: Within our modeling scheme, the explanation for this behavior is found in differing 'rebound' effects after treatment end: simulated drug-mediated inhibition of osteoclastogenesis leads to a build-up of an undifferentiated osteoclast precursor pool.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from the model simulations

claim: After treatment end, the osteoclast precursor pool becomes licensed to differentiate and rapidly gives rise to a large active osteoclast population, leading to accelerated resorption of the bone matrix that had been built up during treatment.
source: After treatment end, this precursor pool becomes licensed to differentiate and rapidly gives rise to a large active osteoclast population, leading to accelerated resorption of the bone matrix that had been built up during treatment.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from the model simulations

claim: Specific drug sequences lead to an attenuation of the rebound effect, for example, by enhancing osteoclast apoptosis during such a 'rebound' phase, thereby modulating bone turnover in the long run.
source: In this paradigm, specific drug sequences lead to an attenuation of this effect, for example, by enhancing osteoclast apoptosis during such a 'rebound' phase, thereby modulating bone turnover in the long run.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from the model simulations

claim: Model analysis suggests considerable potential in the improvement of dosing regimens and drug sequencing in osteoporosis treatment, especially combination therapies, to achieve an optimal effect for a given medication load.
source: In summary, our model analysis suggests considerable potential in the improvement of dosing regimens and drug sequencing in osteoporosis treatment, especially combination therapies, to achieve an optimal effect for a given medication load.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results

claim: The mechanisms of action of one drug may act either favorably or adversely on the state of the bone mineral metabolism left behind by the preceding treatment with another drug.
source: These improvements are possible because the mechanisms of action of one drug may act either favorably or adversely on the state of the bone mineral metabolism left behind by the preceding treatment with another drug.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed differences in treatment outcomes based on model simulations

claim: The effectivity of the modeling approach suggests that—despite the complexity of the bone mineral metabolism—the dynamics relevant for osteoporosis medications can be condensed into only a few components.
source: Our model is built on a small set of essential mechanisms of bone turnover. The effectivity of this approach suggests that—despite the complexity of the bone mineral metabolism—the dynamics relevant for osteoporosis medications can be condensed into only a few components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the success of the simplified model in capturing clinical data

claim: The model can predict the effects of a broad range of drug dosing regimens and complex drug combination therapies beyond those used for model development.
source: Notably, the model can also predict the effects of a broad range of drug dosing regimens and complex drug combination therapies beyond those used for model development.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis

claim: Some parameters (e.g., concentration thresholds for signaling factors) were inferred through the model calibration procedure from BMD and BTM dynamics alone.
source: However, it is important to note that some parameters (e.g., concentration thresholds for signaling factors) were inferred through the model calibration procedure from BMD and BTM dynamics alone.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the model calibration approach

claim: Model simulations extrapolating the long-term BMD development after treatment end suggest that medication schemes eliciting a rapid BMD increase are not necessarily accompanied by a sustained elevation of the BMD.
source: Notably, model simulations extrapolating the long-term BMD development after treatment end suggest that medication schemes eliciting a rapid BMD increase are not necessarily accompanied by a sustained elevation of the BMD.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis

claim: Some initially successful treatment schemes may lead to a 'rebound' effect of accelerated bone loss after treatment end.
source: Instead, some initially successful treatment schemes may lead to a 'rebound' effect of accelerated bone loss after treatment end, a prediction that cautions against using short-term BMD increases as the sole proxy for treatment success.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis

claim: The generic manner in which the model represents bone remodeling and the effects of medications renders it a general platform for the study of treatments that can be adapted to other types of primary and secondary osteoporosis.
source: However, the generic manner in which the model represents bone remodeling and the effects of medications renders it a general platform for the study of treatments that can be adapted to other types of primary and secondary osteoporosis.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications of the model

claim: The modular nature of the model enables future extensions including additional medication types, effects of comorbidities, medications that contribute to osteoporosis, lifestyle-dependent factors, dietary supplementation, and effects of microgravity on bone.
source: The modular nature of the model enables future extensions; besides additional medication types, these may include the effects of comorbidities that elicit osteoporosis or interact with it (such as primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism), medications that contribute to osteoporosis (such as glucocorticoid therapy), lifestyle-dependent factors such as smoking and alcohol consumption, the effects of dietary supplementation of osteoporosis treatment through calcium and vitamin D and effects of microgravity on bone, as experienced by astronauts on extended missions in space.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future extensions of the model

claim: Detailed modeling approaches involving biomechanical feedback suggest synergistic effects between drug treatment of osteoporosis and physical activity.
source: Detailed modeling approaches involving biomechanical feedback suggest synergistic effects between drug treatment of osteoporosis and physical activity (Lavaill et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lavaill et al., 2020

claim: BMD has a prime role in the evaluation of osteoporosis therapies and can be measured rather easily using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
source: While BMD has a prime role in the evaluation of osteoporosis therapies and can be measured rather easily using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), its relationship to fracture risk is complex.
evidence: Draws from established clinical knowledge

claim: The relationship between BMD and fracture risk is complex.
source: While BMD has a prime role in the evaluation of osteoporosis therapies and can be measured rather easily using dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), its relationship to fracture risk is complex.
evidence: Draws from established clinical knowledge

claim: Fracture risk calculations used in clinical practice involve demographic and lifestyle-related factors while mostly relying on BMD point measurements.
source: Fracture risk calculations used in clinical practice also involve demographic and lifestyle-related factors while mostly relying on BMD point measurements (Kanis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanis et al., 2009

claim: Quantitative associations between BMD, age, and fracture risk have been reported in many studies.
source: However, the quantitative associations between BMD, age, and fracture risk reported in many studies (Kanis et al., 2001; Berger et al., 2009; Austin et al., 2012; Krege et al., 2013; Black et al., 2018; Ensrud et al., 2022) can be used to create statistical models that may relate entire BMD time courses to a patient's fracture risk.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on BMD and fracture risk

claim: Statistical models relating BMD time courses to fracture risk can be combined with the physiology-based model to optimize therapies directly for minimized long-term fracture risk instead of maximized BMD gain.
source: Combining such statistical models with the physiology-based model presented here would enable to optimize therapies directly for a minimized long-term fracture risk instead of maximized BMD gain.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential future applications combining the model with statistical approaches

claim: Relative changes in BMD were remarkably consistent among ethnic groups (non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic black, and Mexican American women) despite differing absolute baselines.
source: Rescaling the reported means for the three ethnic groups to their value for the earliest age bin revealed that relative changes in BMD were remarkably consistent among ethnic groups (Appendix 1—figure 1C) despite differing absolute baselines.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the aging dataset from Looker et al., 1998, shown in Appendix 1—figure 1C

claim: The model received only drug dosing information used in the respective clinical trials but was not informed by BMD or BTM measurements during validation.
source: To this end, the model received only drug dosing information used in the respective clinical trials but was not informed by BMD or BTM measurements, which instead it had to predict.
evidence: This describes the validation methodology used in the study

claim: The model was able to predict the complex progression of both BMD and biomarker levels with a high degree of accuracy even in scenarios including sequential treatments with up to three different drug types and parallel treatments with two different drugs.
source: Even in scenarios including sequential treatments with up to three different drug types and parallel treatments with two different drugs, respectively, the model was able to predict the complex progression of both BMD and biomarker levels with a high degree of accuracy (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the validation analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 2
